walkthrough:
Set the scene - pressure generation**
Think of the glomerulus as a tight ball of capillaries fed by a wide afferent arteriole and drained by a narrow efferent arteriole. Because more blood enters than can easily leave, blood / hydrostatic pressure builds up very high inside the glomerulus. That high pressure is the driving force that pushes fluid out of the blood.

First filter - leaky capillary wall**
The glomerular capillary endothelium is fenestrated, meaning it has many large gaps, pores or holes. This makes it much leakier than a normal capillary, so plasma fluid can easily escape. Cells are still too large to fit through in bulk, but fluid and dissolved small solutes can.

Second and third filters - basement membrane and podocytes**
Fluid next meets the basement membrane, a mesh of collagen and glycoprotein fibres. This is the main selective barrier. Outside that are podocytes lining Bowman's capsule. They have interdigitating processes or extensions that wrap the capillaries and leave filtration slits or slit pores between them.

What passes and what stays**
Together the three layers act as an ultrafilter based on size. High pressure forces water, ions, glucose, amino acids and other small solutes out into the Bowman's capsule space as glomerular filtrate. Red and white blood cells, platelets and large plasma proteins with RMM greater than about 68 000 cannot pass and remain in the blood.

Final answer: In the renal corpuscle, the glomerulus has fenestrated endothelium with many large pores. Afferent arteriole is wider than efferent arteriole, creating high hydrostatic / blood pressure in glomerulus, forcing fluid into Bowman's capsule. Podocytes of Bowman's capsule have interdigitating processes forming filtration slits / slit pores. Basement membrane of collagen / glycoprotein mesh acts as main selective filter. Water, ions, glucose and small solutes pass through, while cells and large proteins with RMM > 68 000 do not pass.

walkthrough:
Name the target tissues**
Insulin is released when blood glucose is high and its main targets are liver, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. These are the tissues that can take up large amounts of glucose and convert it to storage forms.

Increase glucose entry**
Insulin increases permeability of these cells to glucose and so increases glucose uptake. It causes intracellular vesicles containing GLUT4 transport proteins to fuse with the cell surface membrane. With more channels in place, more facilitated diffusion of glucose into the cells occurs, especially in muscle and adipose.

Convert glucose to storage molecules**
Inside liver and muscle, insulin stimulates glycogenesis, the synthesis of glycogen from glucose, using enzymes such as glucokinase, hexokinase and glycogen synthase. In liver and adipose it also stimulates synthesis of lipids, triglycerides and fatty acids from glucose. More glucose is also respired, all of which removes free glucose.

Switch off glucose release**
At the same time insulin inhibits processes that would raise blood glucose: glycogenolysis (breakdown of glycogen), gluconeogenesis (formation of glucose from non-carbohydrates) and lipolysis. With uptake and storage increased and release decreased, blood glucose concentration falls back toward normal.

Final answer: Insulin acts on liver, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. It increases glucose uptake by increasing cell permeability, with more GLUT4 transport proteins added by vesicles fusing with cell surface membrane, increasing facilitated diffusion in. It stimulates glycogenesis via glycogen synthase, and lipid / triglyceride / fatty acid synthesis, and increases respiration. It inhibits glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and lipolysis. Net effect is decreased blood glucose concentration.
